Where the R&D is going: NextOS Real Estate

NextOS is Nextwave's AI operating system for small business. Real estate is its first commercial track, built and proven around one working agent at First National Byron Bay. Everything below is the live product as of this week, not a mockup.

The pitch in four sentences

We have built an AI bench that sits behind a working agent and takes on the grunt work of the whole job, not just one corner of it. It wins the rooms: mining the agency’s 93,000-contact CRM (83% of it untouched in six months), scoring every owner with an 18-signal model across four professional data feeds, handing the agent a ranked daily call list with a data-backed reason to ring each person, and turning any appraisal into a magazine-grade digital presentation the same day, where every competitor sends a PDF. Then it runs what she wins: the campaign workspace, the vendor updates, and a marketing playbook where she films 30 seconds and the bench cuts, publishes and amplifies it into automated social advertising. Every monotonous, repeatable task moves onto the bench: built once, licensable to any agent in the country.

1 · The prospecting engine

2,631 contacts pulled from the agency CRM, enriched with property intelligence (Cotality), live buyer and seller intent (realestate.com.au Ignite) and suburb forecasting (HtAG), then scored and ranked. The current cycle holds 665 ranked call cards, served 30 a day, each carrying the one reason that owner is worth a call today. Names blurred here; the agent sees them.

The agent's home screen: today's diary, and the ranked queue with a data-backed hook per contact.

Behind every card: a full dossier

One tap on a card opens the prospect dossier: the owner, the asset, the street, the signal verdict and the play, assembled from the data feeds before the agent rings. Identifying details blurred here; she sees them.

Twenty-four years on title and never once contacted: the kind of owner the model surfaces.

2 · The intelligence map

Every property and suburb in Byron Shire, live: listings, team sales, tenure, valuations, suburb briefings with audio. Hover any pin and it answers; click and the full dossier opens.

The shire at a glance: for-sale, sold, team listings, suburbs and places, one map.

Touch a pin and the whole property answers: the live listing card, one click from the full dossier.

...and every suburb has a dossier of its own

Eleven Shire suburbs carry live dossiers: typical price, weekly rent, gross yield, sales volume, and the agent's own local take, with an audio briefing on tap.

Suffolk Park: a $2.04M typical house, and thirty years of local knowledge in the agent's voice.

3 · The listing workspace

Each listing gets a complete campaign workspace: today's next move, marketing checklist, campaign tracking, enquiries, comparables and media, in one drawer. The system tells the agent what to do next and drafts it for her.

A live campaign: the system has noticed Saturday's open home and is already drafting the vendor update.

4 · Marketing without becoming an influencer

The industry's standard advice to agents is to become a content creator: plan a calendar, front a camera, feed an algorithm. Our agent has no interest in being an influencer; she wants to sell houses. So the bench reduces marketing to a short checklist per listing: she films 30 seconds on her phone, and the AI team cuts, captions and publishes the rest.

The per-listing marketing checklist: one small human act per line, the machine does the remainder.

Next: the listing goes everywhere by itself

That checklist is the seed of the next stage of the build. The listing's own photos become short-form video, the video becomes Instagram and Meta placements, and the campaign is assembled, launched and reported without the agent ever opening an ad manager: modern digital advertising, automated behind one tick-box, amplifying every listing across the web. The direction of the whole track is the same: prospecting and the proposal are only the first part. Every monotonous, repeatable task an agent carries moves onto the bench, one checklist line at a time.

5 · The win-the-room weapon

A real appraisal turned into a same-day branded digital presentation: comparables, market position, pricing strategy. The agent we back converts 66.7% of the appraisals she sits. This gets her into more rooms, sharper in every one.

7/31 Hayters Drive, Suffolk Park: the same-day pitch a vendor opens on their phone.

The evidence pages

Every presentation is built on settled sales, each one adjusted to the subject home, and a pricing position the agent can defend line by line.

Eight comparable sales, each price-adjusted against the subject property.

6 · The bench itself

The product is not one tool, it is a staffed AI team: sales, marketing, customer service, research, signal-scouting, each seat with a name, a voice and a job. The agent talks to them like colleagues. This same chassis is what we license.

  • Anna · Principal, the human. Wins the room; the bench carries the rest.
  • Reggie · EA and the voice of the bench. Say it, she routes it: the diary, the dossiers, the day’s queue.
  • Ryan · Sales. Owns the pipeline; every follow-up on time, nothing goes cold.
  • Dax · Closer. The sharp end of appraisal-to-exclusive: the firm move drafted so it can be delivered soft.
  • Cleo · Marketing. Turns 30 seconds of phone video into reels, captions and campaigns.
  • Holly · Customer service. Vendors and buyers looked after: updates, bookings, reviews.
  • Scout · Signal scout. Watches the market feeds for price cuts, stale campaigns and withdrawn listings.
  • Daphne · Research. Builds the dossiers, comparables and suburb intel behind every card.

Eight seats on the bench: one human principal, seven AI colleagues, each one a phone call away.

Nurture to sold: the funnel the whole system exists to fill.

Why this is an asset, not a burn

  • Platform economics. Nearly all spend to date is build-once: the scoring model, the data integrations, the presentation engine, the app itself. Agent number two costs hosting and data, not development.
  • The category is validated. Luxury Presence (US) and NurtureCloud (built by Ray White, AU) prove agents and agencies pay for exactly this. Nobody sells it to individual agents in Australia yet.
  • The unit maths is short. One Byron Shire listing carries roughly $30–50K in gross commission. The engine needs to influence only a handful of listings a year to return the track's entire annual run cost. Current outgoings are data APIs, AI compute and hosting: monthly, cancellable, nothing locked in.

The proof gate and the next 90 days

  • Convert the live pipeline into the first signed listing demonstrably sourced by the engine. That is the only milestone that matters right now.
  • Package the per-agent licence (monthly SaaS) with that first listing as the case study.
  • Then, and only then, the invest-further and pricing decision, made on evidence.
